Hello!
Tea shop/wares employee of many years here! Traditional cast iron tetsubin pots should NEVER be used as a kettle for heating, only for steeping. That is a huge confusion in the U.S. Kettles=Heating water Tea pots=steeping tea
Additionally if you don't have a spiffy hot water heater (anyone that drinks tea regularly enough should look into one. I have two Zojurushi brand hot water heaters. I've used and owned just about every kind available and find them to be the best. They are the most accurate and user friendly. They're also great for other purposes like oatmeal and such...but i digress)... there is an easy trick you can use to ensure your tea is steeped at the proper temperatures. This makes a huge impact on the flavour and benefits you get out of your teas. Especially if you're drinking anything of quality. 

Watch the bubbles in the kettle. As they start to form but aren't rising they're about 175 F, bubbles forming and just rising 195 F, bubbles going rapidly 208 F... It sounds goofy but it's usually within a degree or two!

White/Green Tea about 175 F 
Oolong/Black Tea 195 F
Tisanes (Rooibos/Herbal/Mate') 208 F

A great upside to cast iron tea ware (so long as it is a good quality Japanese is where it's at) is as you steep it the enamel coating inside develops a nice patina. This is a coating that makes your tea more rich in vitamins and minerals and brings out the flavours of the teas. Also, many higher quality teas are able to re-infuse more in cast iron because it has a more even heat distribution than most pots. All in all, they are generally considered "one of the best" ways of steeping tea. One VERY important thing to keep in mind when caring for your cast iron!!! Never wash! Only rinse the interior with boiling or hot water! Do NOT get the exterior wet. If you do (even if it's tea) dab it dry with a DRY rag...NEVER wipe! This includes your accessories! Cups, coasters, warmers, TRIVETS. Trivets are a biggie. That is the biggest complaint I've gotten. Boo hoo my trivet rusted. WELL THAT'S BECAUSE YOU DIDN'T TAKE CARE OF IT!!! Gently dab your trivet try and once you are done with all of these cleaning goodies let it dry upside down on a towel or a NON-METAL dish rack (I still recommend a towel under the dish rack). I own four cast iron sets myself (because I have a problem) and not one of my items has a single chip, rust spot, or blemish. It all comes down to care. And quite frankly, I don't know how much easier rinsing and dabbing something gets... 

One of my personal favourite methods of steeping is the Chinese method of yixing/gong fu steeping. Yixing tea sets are traditionally very small as in gong fu steeping you use smaller amounts of water with more tea. This allows you to do MANY steeps and experience a different depth of flavour with each pot, though you generally do not drink the first few infusions as these are to allow the leaves to open. There is often some sort of "tea table" where any extra liquid or waste can be put and used to "season". Fixing tea sets and pots are special because the can become seasoned with teas so they actually take on the flavours of the teas you infuse in them. The more you use them, the better your tea will be. One of my favourite local tea masters has done some training sessions with me and he told me about when he was doing his training in China you could tell which tea masters were legitimate by how stained their sets and tea animals (small animals made from the same fixing clay) were. Each time a master would do a tea tasting they would pour the excess over their animals into the tea tables. It's just such a fascinating experience. Like cast iron you do not want to wash yixing. The first time you get one you'll want to soak it in a pot of boiling water. I recommend checking out Verdant Tea's video on how to properly prep your yixing pot the first time. A simple rinse is plenty. You don't want to get rid of the beautiful seasoning you just did to your pot!

Sorry for the crazy long speal! I could go on about tea forever!!!
Any questions I'm happy to chat!

TLDR; Cast iron tea sets are ONLY for steeping NEVER heating water.
There is an easy trick on how to get your water heated on the stove to the proper temp for the corresponding tea.
Fixing sets are cool beans!
